found.domain: falsification-H1-to-H4 (cross-domain falsifier: missing facts vs interpretation; recurrence; existing encoding; legal/organisational discretion)
found.domain_assessment:
NETWORK CAVEAT FIRST: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before this finder ran, and the egress proxy blocked every non-GitHub host tried (28 domains: oig.hhs.gov, kff.org, ecfr.gov, govinfo.gov, federalregister.gov, cms.gov, uscis.gov, ssa.gov, cbp.gov, gao.gov, irs.gov, dol.gov, law.cornell.edu, justia, courtlistener, bailii, legislation.gov.uk, gov.uk, eur-lex, curia, edpb, artificialintelligenceact.eu, gdpr-info.eu, naic.org, ama-assn.org, financial-ombudsman.org.uk, ipsacompliance.org.uk, assets.ctfassets.net, fanniemae, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, web.archive.org, archive.ph, api.openalex.org, api.crossref.org, arxiv.org, wikipedia). What WAS obtained: (a) one primary industry-association document already in the scratchpad (AHIP, 'Improving Prior Authorization for Patients & Providers', June 2025, survey of 32 commercial plans = 109M lives); (b) the hash-verified coding of all 46 IPSA Compliance Officer review PDFs held in the local repo (primary court/tribunal-type documents, coded by two independent passes, kappa 0.78-1.0); (c) ~20 successful GitHub fetches, including a 1,533-decision corpus of UK Financial Ombudsman insurance claim decisions (2024-01 to 2026-07, 183 firms) with a tagged taxonomy of why insurer declines were overturned, a FOS 'precedent consistency' tool with test results, the OpenFisca-France and DGFiP mlang rules-as-code repos and their interpretation issues, a community Rules-as-Code guide, and PubLedge (an open protocol for recording fact-specific interpretations). Legal authorities for H4 (Firestone v. Bruch; 42 CFR 422.566(d) and 422.101(b)(6); EU AI Act Art. 14 and Annex III; GDPR Art. 22 and CJEU C-634/21 SCHUFA; IRC 6110(k)(3); 19 CFR 177.9; British Oxygen fettering doctrine) could not be fetched and are cited from analyst knowledge with URLs, flagged UNVERIFIED IN SESSION; no operational statistics from blocked sources are asserted as facts.

VERDICTS. H1 (missing facts, not ambiguity): PARTIALLY SUPPORTED, domain-dependent. In prior authorisation the payer trade body itself says initial denials 'are often a result of incomplete information from providers' and 45-47% of requests still arrive by phone/fax/mail (AHIP 2025) - category A dominant. But in the two appeal/complaint corpora with sourced distributions, missing evidence is a minor primary driver (IPSA: 2 of 46 primary issues; FOS insurance: 10 of 626 upheld = 1.6%) while 16-20 of 46 IPSA outcomes still turned on facts gathered AFTER the original decision. The bigger finding is that in both corpora the dominant driver is neither A nor H: it is discretion/exception requests (IPSA 18 of 46) and handling/process/communication/quantum (FOS: 45.2% of upheld; policy-wording interpretation only 2.6%). H1 is therefore right that H is small, but wrong about why: the residual is discretion and handling, which is worse for the product than missing facts.

H2 (ambiguity repeats too rarely to compound): SUPPORTED at the granularity where disputes actually arise, NOT SUPPORTED at coarse class level. IPSA 1,000-claim recurrence: one settlement per class covers 93% at category+cost-type (67 classes, 22% of settlements never reused) but 37% at what-was-bought (633 classes, 86% seen once). FOS: only 16 policy-wording overturns in 1,349 claim decisions across 183 firms in 2.5 years (about 0.09 per firm), so wording ambiguity reaching the ombudsman is rare and thinly spread. Counter-evidence: the FOS 'precedent' tool found a comparable published decision for 100% of tested affordability complaints (73% aligned, 14% misaligned, 13% divided precedent), showing that in a narrow, high-volume complaint type precedent does cover cases; and a Rules-as-Code guide states 'over time judgements accrue, which can provide patterns you can encode'. The 13% 'divided precedent' rate is simultaneously evidence for H4 (settlement does not converge).

H3 (organisations already encode settlements adequately): PARTIALLY SUPPORTED / MIXED. Formal channels exist wherever a body has rule-making power: IPSA revises the Scheme (18th edition lifted the newsletter ban); DGFiP encodes the entire income-tax computation annually in its M language; French benefit rules are encoded in OpenFisca-France with semantic versioning and a changelog; CMS now requires MA plans' internal coverage criteria to be public and reviewed annually by a UM committee (unverified in session); CBP rulings are binding and published (unverified). But speed and completeness are poor: IPSA committed to only 4 of 17 recommended rule/guidance changes; OpenFisca-France interpretation issues stay open for years (#1618 open since Aug 2021, #1554 since Jun 2021, #1829 since Mar 2022); mlang notes DGFiP never published part of its computation logic. PubLedge's claim that interpretations 'live in scattered, unstructured records' is an unadopted (0-star) open-source claim, i.e. weak. Net: the gap is real but it is a gap in WHO IS EMPOWERED to ratify and HOW FAST, not a gap in encoding tooling - the same conclusion the prior investigation reached.

H4 (interpretation stays discretionary after precedent): SUPPORTED for adverse decisions about individuals in regulated consumer domains (US and EU), NOT SUPPORTED for favourable decisions and for B2B/internal operational decisions. Sourced: AHIP reports 100% of responding plans use no AI/algorithm to deny medical-necessity requests without clinician review and commit that all such denials be reviewed by a licensed clinician; IPSA Scheme s.2.3 says a determination binds no later claim; 5 of 46 reviews expressly disclaim precedent and 22 of 46 still contain a general reading the reviewer cannot make binding; 'it was paid before' was argued in 24-26 of 46 and rejected in 15; FOS 'divided precedent' 13%. Unverified-in-session legal authorities point the same way for denials/adverse decisions: 42 CFR 422.566(d) physician review; ERISA Firestone deference is to the administrator's discretion, not to precedent; GDPR Art. 22 plus SCHUFA; EU AI Act Art. 14 human oversight for Annex III uses (benefits eligibility, creditworthiness, life/health insurance risk, employment), applying from Aug 2026; UK/Commonwealth fettering-of-discretion doctrine. Crucially, these constraints bind DENIALS and adverse decisions; approvals can be automated (AHIP: ~20% of medical PAs already approved in real time, target 80% by 2027) and importer-specific customs rulings and IRS revenue rulings are prospectively binding. So H4 does not kill a settlement ledger; it restricts it to the approve side of consumer-facing workflows and to non-consumer workflows.

OVERALL for the falsification cluster: the strongest sourced pattern across three independent corpora (IPSA n=46, FOS n=1,349, IPSA recurrence n=1,000) is that once bright-line rules and after-the-fact audit are in place, the human work that remains is dominated by discretion on unique facts and by handling quality, with rule-meaning disputes at 2.6% (FOS) to 26% (IPSA) and prospective settlement power scarce. Any team continuing should treat H2 and H4 as the live threats and run the brief's base-rate experiment on a workflow where (i) the decision owner also holds rule-making power, (ii) the settled cases are approvals not denials, and (iii) the class granularity at which disputes arise is coarse.

workflows.name: H1 falsification: missing facts vs interpretive ambiguity (prior authorisation, immigration RFEs, expenses appeals, insurance complaints)
workflows.geography: US (prior auth, immigration), UK (IPSA expenses, FOS insurance complaints)
workflows.decision_volume: Prior auth: AHIP 2024 member survey - 93% of commercial medical claims and 96% of drug claims NOT subject to PA; ~97% of medical and ~90% of drug PA requests ultimately approved; ~20% of medical PAs approved in real time (industry association; local copy scratchpad/ahip_pa.pdf, https://www.ahip.org, June 2025). IPSA: 82,787 claims/yr in full file, 46 published appeal reviews 2011-2025 (court/tribunal-type primary docs, repo results/corpus_study.json; source page https://www.ipsacompliance.org.uk/investigations/completed-reviews). FOS insurance claim decisions: 1,533 published decisions 2024-01-08 to 2026-07-21, 1,349 claim decisions from 183 firms (third-party corpus of tribunal-type primary decisions, https://github.com/SwayamBhageria/claims-overturn-bench).
workflows.human_review_rate: Prior auth: 100% of PA requests are human/clinician-touched on the denial side by plan commitment; ~20% approved in real time (AHIP 2025, industry association). IPSA: 997 paid / 1 not paid / 2 repaid of 1,000 sampled claims - pre-payment refusal near zero (repo results, primary IPSA data). FOS: 46.4% of insurance claim complaints upheld against the insurer (626/1,349) (GitHub corpus of FOS decisions).
workflows.why_humans_review: SOURCED DISTRIBUTIONS. IPSA 46 reviews, primary issue (agreed/adjudicated): E/G discretion-or-exception 18 (39%), C rule meaning 12 (26%), process/advice 5 (11%), B fact characterisation 4 (9%), A evidence sufficiency 2 (4%), version timing 1, disputed 3, other 1; but 16-20 of 46 outcomes relied on facts gathered after the original decision (A in disguise). FOS 626 upheld: handling family (process 125, communication 121, quantum 70, delay 30) = 45.2%; misrepresentation/non-disclosure (B/C under CIDRA) 7.5%; policy wording (C/H) 2.6% = 16 cases; evidence (A) 1.6%; fraud 1.1%; untagged 49%. Prior auth: AHIP states initial denials 'are often a result of incomplete information from providers' (A), no share given. ESTIMATE (mine, from these): A 5-40% by domain (highest in prior auth/immigration), B 5-10%, C 3-25%, E/G 20-40%, H at most a subset of C, i.e. 2-15%.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: IPSA: 22-24 of 46 reviews state a general reading that would decide future similar claims; 17 recommend a rule/guidance change; IPSA committed to 4; Scheme s.2.3 says a determination does not bind future claims; 5 reviews expressly disclaim precedent.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: court or tribunal (46 primary PDFs, hash-verified in repo; page itself blocked this session)
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Only via a separate Scheme edition change (4 of 46 disputes led to one); the reviewer cannot bind.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Prior auth: AHIP says PA criteria are developed by plan medical professionals with P&T and utilisation-management committees and that plans 'regularly review and adjust their prior authorization lists based on current data' - i.e. committee-owned criteria updated periodically, not case-by-case settlement.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Criteria lists and coverage policies; case denials themselves are reviewed individually by clinicians.

workflows.economic_pain: FOS ombudsman case fee is £680 per case regardless of outcome (GitHub corpus README citing FOS fee; industry cost per escalated review). Median FOS award where the claim stood £250, where disturbed £200 (same corpus). IPSA median amount in a published dispute £584, 30 of 45 under £1,000 (repo results). Prior-auth labour cost figures (AMA survey) could not be fetched (ama-assn.org blocked).
workflows.existing_solutions: Prior auth: payer UM platforms and committee-maintained clinical criteria; FHIR ePA standards by 2027 (AHIP). Expenses: IPSA online claims system plus published Scheme editions and guidance. Insurance complaints: firm complaint-handling teams; FOS publishes all decisions; a GitHub tool ('precedent') already checks a handler's proposed outcome against comparable published FOS decisions (73% aligned, 14% misaligned, 13% divided precedent, 0% no comparable precedent in tests; https://github.com/Zubindeepak14/precedent). None captures settlements as versioned executable precedents; FOS decisions are not binding precedent.
workflows.buyer_and_budget: Not applicable to a falsification entry; see domain finders.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: Prior auth medical-necessity denials require clinician review (AHIP commitment; 42 CFR 422.566(d) for MA - unverified in session). FOS decides on what is 'fair and reasonable'; decisions bind only the parties.
workflows.notes: H1 verdict: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED. Missing facts dominate in prior auth (qualitative, trade body) and plausibly immigration RFEs (USCIS data blocked; note from analyst memory, UNVERIFIED: H-1B RFE rates swung from ~40% in FY2019 to ~10% in FY2022 with the 2017 memo and its 2021 rescission, which would mean RFE rates are driven by adjudication policy, not applicant omissions - verify at https://www.uscis.gov/tools/reports-and-studies/immigration-and-citizenship-data). In appeal corpora, missing evidence is a small primary driver but later-gathered facts still decide a third of outcomes; the dominant residual is discretion and handling, not interpretation.

workflows.name: H2 falsification: does interpretive ambiguity recur enough to compound? (expenses, insurance complaints, affordability complaints, agent permissions)
workflows.geography: UK (IPSA, FOS); owner's own agent permission log
workflows.decision_volume: IPSA: 1,000-claim sample of 82,787 (2023-24) analysed at five granularities (repo results/recurrence.json, primary IPSA data). FOS: 1,349 insurance claim decisions, 183 firms, 2.5 years (https://github.com/SwayamBhageria/claims-overturn-bench). Owner's coding-agent log: 9,404 tool calls (prior_evidence.md, repo).
workflows.why_humans_review: Recurrence, not cause, is at issue here. Sourced: IPSA G2 (category+cost type): 67 classes, 93.3% covered, 22.4% of settlements never reused, median 5 claims per settlement, 29 settlements to cover 90%. G5 (normalised item text): 633 classes, 36.7% covered, 86.1% never reused, median 1-2 claims per settlement. FOS: policy-wording as primary ground in 16 of 1,349 claim decisions (1.2%) across 183 firms and 9 product lines = about 0.09 wording disputes per firm in 2.5 years; the corpus README gives no cross-firm recurrence of identical wording issues. Agent permissions: 906 settlements cover 90% of 9,404 calls, 47.5% never reused, median 2 later calls (prior_evidence).

settlement_loop_evidence.description: FOS 'precedent' consistency tool (affordability / irresponsible-lending complaints): every tested proposed outcome had a factually comparable published FOS decision; 73% aligned, 14% misaligned, 13% divided precedent. Evidence that in a narrow high-volume complaint type, precedent exists and covers cases, but that precedent itself is divided in 1 of 8 cases.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Advisory consistency check only; FOS decisions are not binding on later complaints.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Community Rules-as-Code guide: 'Judgement-based rules are ones that require someone accountable to make a judgement' and are less appropriate for RaC; 'Over time judgements accrue, which can provide patterns you can encode, such as if you meet criteria x, y and z, then the judgement is likely n'. This is the Sophon thesis stated by practitioners, with the caveat that it works only when patterns emerge.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: industry/community guide (Digital Aotearoa, Cardano Rules-as-Code project; NOT an official NZ government document)
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Encode accrued judgements as likelihood patterns; no operational data given.

workflows.economic_pain: Compounding requires reuse; sourced reuse medians are 5 (coarse) to 1-2 (fine) later cases per settlement in expenses, 2 in agent permissions. FOS case fee £680 per escalated case (corpus README) bounds the value of avoiding one escalation.
workflows.existing_solutions: Bright-line limits plus after-the-fact audit already govern 99.9% of IPSA claims; FOS publishes decisions; consistency-check tools exist as open source.
workflows.notes: H2 verdict: SUPPORTED at the granularity where disputes actually arise (fine classes, 86% singletons; wording disputes 1.2% of FOS claim decisions), NOT SUPPORTED at coarse class level, where repetition is plentiful but policy owners already use bright lines. The one counter-signal (100% precedent coverage in affordability complaints) comes from a narrow complaint type with statutory tests and a single national adjudicator; it should be probed by a domain finder, not taken as general.

workflows.name: H3 falsification: once settled, do organisations already encode it adequately? (French benefits/tax rules-as-code, IPSA Scheme editions, MA coverage criteria, customs/IRS rulings)
workflows.geography: France (OpenFisca-France, DGFiP M), UK (IPSA), US (CMS/MA, CBP, IRS - unverified in session)
workflows.decision_volume: OpenFisca-France: full French tax and benefit system as executable code, semantic versioning, changelog per change (https://github.com/openfisca/openfisca-france). DGFiP: entire income-tax computation published yearly as M source (2018-2022 versions referenced; https://github.com/MLanguage/mlang). IPSA: 46 disputes, 17 recommended changes, 4 committed (repo). MA: CMS-4201-F requires internal coverage criteria to be public with evidence and reviewed annually by a UM committee (42 CFR 422.101(b)(6); UNVERIFIED in session, ecfr.gov and federalregister.gov blocked).
workflows.why_humans_review: n/a for H3; the question is speed/completeness of encoding. Sourced: OpenFisca-France issues that turn on administrative interpretation remain open for years: #1618 'Normalisation des métadonnées des variables' open since 2 Aug 2021; #1554 'Mise à jour de la Majoration Tierce Personne' open since 15 Jun 2021; #1829 'Erreur pour le paramètre indemnité accident travail' open since 24 Mar 2022; #2403 open since Dec 2024; #1426 (DOM one-child degressive supplement) was a legal-reading question the contributor asked maintainers to ratify before coding (https://github.com/openfisca/openfisca-france/issues/1426). mlang: DGFiP 'has not published the source code' for the iterative part of the computation, so the reverse-engineers wrote M++ to encode unpublished logic.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: OpenFisca-France issue #1426: contributor identifies that Art. L.755-12 CSS excludes the degressive family-allowance supplement for DOM one-child households, OpenFisca was paying 10.4 EUR, contributor offers a PR 'if maintainers agree with the legal interpretation' - an interpretation ratified by code maintainers, not by CNAF.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: open-source rules-as-code issue tracker (moderate; primary record of the encoding decision)
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Becomes code for all later simulations; provenance is a GitHub issue, not an administrative ruling.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: IPSA: Davies review reports the newsletter rule changed in the 18th Scheme edition; Aquarone review records IPSA's stated intention to clarify festive-hospitality guidance; overall 4 of 17 recommended changes committed.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: court or tribunal (primary PDF, hash-verified in repo; host blocked this session)
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Scheme edition change; case remedies expressly non-precedential.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: PubLedge: open protocol (v0.2.x, 140 commits, 0 stars) to record 'fact-specific written interpretations between two parties' (PLRs, no-action letters, advisory opinions, HOA decisions) in structured markdown with SHA-256; asserts such interpretations 'live in scattered, unstructured records that can't be compared across authorities'; does not version or link interpretations to later cases.

workflows.economic_pain: Not quantifiable from reachable sources. Signal of inadequacy: multi-year open interpretation issues in a national benefit codebase; 13 of 17 IPSA recommendations not committed.
workflows.existing_solutions: Rules-as-code (OpenFisca, Catala - 'faithful-by-construction algorithms from legislative texts' with default logic for exceptions, lawyer-readable PDFs, Inria research project, 'unstable'; https://github.com/CatalaLang/catala), DGFiP M language, versioned scheme editions, published coverage criteria (MA, mandated), binding published rulings (CBP CROSS, 19 CFR 177.9; IRS revenue rulings, with PLRs non-precedential under IRC 6110(k)(3) - both UNVERIFIED in session). An open-source FOS consistency checker and an RFE-analysis prompt set (classifies USCIS issues into Evidence Gap / Legal Argument / Policy Interpretation / Credibility, no counts; https://github.com/AIStack-Legal/rfe-analysis) exist but do not capture versioned executable settlements.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: Where a regulator mandates publication of internal criteria (MA, CMS-4201-F, unverified) encoding becomes compulsory and the gap closes by regulation rather than product.
workflows.notes: H3 verdict: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED / MIXED. Formal encoding channels exist wherever the settling body has rule-making power and are exercised (scheme editions, annual tax code, published rulings). Encoding is slow and incomplete where the settler lacks power or the codebase is community-maintained (years-old open issues; 4 of 17 committed). The deficiency is governance authority and cadence, not tooling; a product would need to supply ratification power it cannot itself confer.

workflows.name: H4 falsification: does interpretation stay legally or organisationally discretionary after precedent? (health denials, ERISA, EU AI Act/GDPR, benefits, expenses, ombudsman)
workflows.decision_volume: AHIP survey: 32 commercial plans (109M lives), 21 Medicaid plans (53% of enrolment), 21 MA plans (42% of enrolment), Oct 2024 (industry association, local copy). IPSA 46 reviews (primary). FOS 1,349 decisions (GitHub corpus of primary decisions).
workflows.human_review_rate: AHIP: 100% of responding plans report no AI/algorithm denials of medical-necessity PA requests without clinician review; commitment that 'all prior authorization denials based on medical necessity for clinical factors will be reviewed by a licensed and qualified clinician' - 'reflects existing practices and is in effect now'. Approval side: ~20% of medical PAs approved in real time today, target at least 80% of approvals real-time by 2027 (AHIP June 2025).
workflows.why_humans_review: Legal/organisational mandates, not epistemic need. SOURCED: IPSA Scheme s.2.3 - a determination on one claim does not bind future similar claims (17th edition PDF, hash-verified in repo); 5 of 46 reviews expressly disclaim precedent; 2 reviews (Snell, Frith) state a general reading AND disclaim precedent; 'paid before / staff advice' argued in 24-26 of 46, rejected 15, accepted 5, partly 4; two same-year reviews treat 19 and 25 prior payments in opposite ways (Pound vs McDonagh). FOS consistency tool: 13% 'divided precedent'. UNVERIFIED IN SESSION (analyst knowledge, hosts blocked): Firestone Tire & Rubber Co. v. Bruch, 489 U.S. 101 (1989) - ERISA denials reviewed de novo unless the plan grants the administrator discretionary authority, in which case abuse-of-discretion review applies (https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/489/101); 42 CFR 422.566(d) - MA medical-necessity adverse determinations must be reviewed by a physician or other appropriate professional with expertise (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-422/subpart-M/section-422.566); GDPR Art. 22 right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal/similar effect, with human-intervention safeguard (https://gdpr-info.eu/art-22-gdpr/), extended by CJEU C-634/21 SCHUFA (7 Dec 2023) to credit scoring a lender 'draws strongly' on (https://curia.europa.eu); EU AI Act Reg. 2024/1689 Art. 14 human oversight incl. automation-bias awareness and power to override/interrupt, for Annex III uses incl. public-benefit eligibility, creditworthiness, life/health insurance risk assessment and pricing, employment decisions, obligations applying from 2 Aug 2026 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689); UK/Commonwealth fettering-of-discretion doctrine, British Oxygen Co v Board of Trade [1971] AC 610 - a policy is permitted but the decision-maker 'must always be willing to listen to anyone with something new to say'; Australia Robodebt Royal Commission (July 2023) on unlawful automated benefit decisions (https://robodebt.royalcommission.gov.au/publications/report).

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Binding prospective settlements DO exist where the settler has statutory power, cutting against H4 in non-consumer domains: CBP ruling letters are binding on CBP for the described transactions and revoked only by notice (19 CFR 177.9, 19 USC 1625(c)); IRS revenue rulings are precedential while PLRs are not (IRC 6110(k)(3)); SSA Social Security Rulings bind adjudicators. ALL UNVERIFIED IN SESSION.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Published ruling database (CROSS); importer may rely; third parties may cite.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: MA internal coverage criteria: CMS-4201-F (2023) permits internal criteria only where Medicare criteria are not fully established, requires them to be publicly accessible with evidence summaries and reviewed annually by a UM committee - a regulator-mandated settlement loop from denial practice to published criteria. UNVERIFIED IN SESSION.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Published criteria applied to later requests; individual denials still need physician review.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: AHIP plans' voluntary commitments (June 2025): standardised FHIR ePA data by 2027; 80% of approvals real-time by 2027; clinician review of every medical-necessity denial. Approvals are being automated; denials are being kept human by design.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Criteria-driven auto-approval; denial path remains discretionary and human.

workflows.economic_pain: FOS case fee £680 per escalated complaint (GitHub corpus README). Cost of mandated clinician review of PA denials not obtainable from reachable sources (AMA survey blocked).
workflows.existing_solutions: Human-in-the-loop denial review mandated by law/commitment; auto-approval engines on the favourable side; published criteria/rulings where the body has rule-making power.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: See why_humans_review. In the EU, Annex III high-risk systems for creditworthiness, insurance risk, benefits and employment carry Art. 14 human-oversight duties from Aug 2026; in the US, state UR laws and 42 CFR 422.566(d) require physician review of medical-necessity denials (state statutes not fetched).
workflows.notes: H4 verdict: SUPPORTED for adverse/denial decisions about individuals in health, credit, benefits, employment and insurance (US and EU) and for any body whose own rules say determinations do not bind (IPSA, FOS). NOT SUPPORTED for approvals/favourable decisions, and for B2B or internal operational decisions (customs rulings, tax rulings, access grants, procurement exceptions) where statutory or organisational power makes settlements binding. Consequence for the product: a settlement ledger can lawfully automate only the approve side of consumer-facing workflows; denials stay human regardless of precedent.

workflows.name: Cross-check domain: UK insurance claim complaints at the Financial Ombudsman (as a falsification instrument, not a candidate)
workflows.decision_volume: 1,533 published FOS insurance decisions 2024-01-08 to 2026-07-21; 1,349 claim decisions after excluding 126 non-claim disputes; 183 firms; FOS search totals 2024-01-01 to 2026-08-31 by product: motor 4,885, buildings 3,561, travel 2,466, warranty 1,629, pet 856 (https://github.com/SwayamBhageria/claims-overturn-bench, third-party corpus built from FOS published decisions; FOS site itself blocked).
workflows.human_review_rate: 100% of escalated complaints are ombudsman-decided; uphold rate 46.4% overall; by product warranty 52.6%, buildings 46.4%, contents 46.1%, motor 44.5%, travel 43.6%, pet 43.5%, home 42.9%, mobile 40.5%, gadget 38.0% (same corpus).
workflows.why_humans_review: Of 626 upheld: process 20.0%, communication 19.3%, quantum 11.2%, misrepresentation 7.5%, delay 4.8%, policy wording 2.6%, evidence 1.6%, fraud 1.1%, untagged 49.0% (rules-based tagging, each tag traced to a sentence). 28.6% of upheld cases left the decline intact but faulted the process; 71.4% changed the payment. My mapping: handling/process = not A-H at all (service quality), misrepresentation = B/C, policy wording = C/H (2.6%), evidence = A (1.6%).

settlement_loop_evidence.description: FOS decisions are published in full and used by an open-source consistency checker for complaint handlers; FOS also publishes 'our approach' guidance (not fetched). Decisions bind only the parties.

workflows.economic_pain: FOS case fee £680 per case to the firm; median award £200-250 (corpus README).
workflows.existing_solutions: Firm complaint teams; FOS publication; open-source consistency tools.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: FOS statutory 'fair and reasonable' standard; not bound by its own prior decisions.
workflows.notes: Third-party corpus, so treat the taxonomy as moderate not strong; but it is built from primary FOS decisions with traceable tags and is the only sourced why-overturned distribution reachable this session. Policy-wording interpretation at 2.6% of upheld (1.2% of all claim decisions) is the single strongest datapoint against the thesis in insurance claims.

evidence_against_thesis: IPSA (46 primary appeal reviews, two-pass coding): primary issue was discretionary relief/exception in 18, rule meaning in 12, evidence sufficiency in 2; 16-20 outcomes relied on facts gathered after the original decision; Scheme s.2.3 says a determination binds no later claim; 5 reviews expressly disclaim precedent; IPSA committed to 4 of 17 recommended rule changes; 'paid before' rejected in 15 of 24-26. Source: repo results/corpus_study.json built from https://www.ipsacompliance.org.uk/investigations/completed-reviews (court/tribunal-type).

IPSA recurrence (1,000 real claims): at the granularity where disputes arise, 633 classes, 86% seen once, one settlement covers 37%; coverage is high only at coarse classes already governed by bright lines. Source: repo results/recurrence.json (primary IPSA data).

FOS insurance claim decisions 2024-2026 (1,349 claim decisions, 183 firms): policy-wording interpretation is the primary ground in only 16 upheld cases (2.6% of upheld, 1.2% of all); handling/process/communication/quantum/delay account for 45.2% of upheld; evidence only 1.6%. Source: https://github.com/SwayamBhageria/claims-overturn-bench (third-party corpus of primary decisions).

refuted.claim: H3: 'OpenFisca-France issues that turn on administrative interpretation remain open for years: #1618 (Aug 2021), #1554 (Jun 2021), #1829 (Mar 2022), #2403 (Dec 2024)'.
refuted.why: Fetched each issue. #1618 is an RFC on normalising variable/parameter metadata (unit, reference fields) for IPP/LexImpact display, not a legal reading (https://github.com/openfisca/openfisca-france/issues/1618). #2403 is about harmonising sign conventions of income-tax variables (iai, cehr, pfu) for code readability (https://github.com/openfisca/openfisca-france/issues/2403). #1554 is a stale parameter value: the MTP amount effective 1 Apr 2021 per a CNAV circular had not been keyed in (https://github.com/openfisca/openfisca-france/issues/1554). #1829 is a parameter-value discrepancy against Legifrance (416.47 vs 411.12 for 2003) (https://github.com/openfisca/openfisca-france/issues/1829). None is an interpretation question; they are metadata hygiene and parameter freshness (closer to brief category A/B than C/H). The single genuine legal-reading issue the finder cited, #1426 (Art. L.755-12 CSS), was opened 16 Apr 2020 and is closed (listing shows Feb 2021, roughly 10 months) (https://github.com/openfisca/openfisca-france/issues/1426). The CHANGELOG shows version 176.1.0 (May 2026) and roughly 40-50 releases in the last 12 months, about 2-4 per week (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openfisca/openfisca-france/master/CHANGELOG.md). Encoding cadence in the French rules-as-code case is fast, not slow; the finder's evidence for 'slow and incomplete encoding' collapses to one 10-month issue plus IPSA's 4 of 17.

refuted.claim: H4/H2: 'FOS consistency tool found 13% divided precedent, i.e. the adjudicator's own settlements do not converge'.
refuted.why: The tool's pre-registration defines 'divided_precedent' as a retrieved neighbourhood whose plurality vote falls below a 'majority_floor' threshold, and that threshold was chosen by constrained optimisation to keep decided_rate >= 0.85 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Zubindeepak14/precedent/main/docs/majority_floor_prereg.md). The 13% is therefore close to the abstention budget selected by design (max 15%), not a measurement of Financial Ombudsman inconsistency. Retrieval is factor-vector similarity over structured fields with an optional Haiku rerank, and verdict-level upheld recall is 0.4138, so neighbourhoods are noisy (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Zubindeepak14/precedent/main/README.md). The repo has 0 stars, 0 forks, 2 commits, and states 'Cursor wrote the code' (https://github.com/Zubindeepak14/precedent). The inversion test does show alignment is a genuine comparison (aligned 75% -> 14% when the proposal is flipped, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Zubindeepak14/precedent/main/docs/inversion_test.md), which rescues the '100% comparable precedent found' observation, but not the 13% as evidence for H4.

refuted.claim: Cross-check/H1: 'Policy-wording interpretation at 2.6% of upheld (1.2% of all) is the single strongest datapoint against the thesis in insurance claims'.
refuted.why: The policy_wording tag is a regex over four phrasings: 'exclusion (does not|didn't) apply', 'ambiguous', 'contra proferentem', 'term (is|was) (unclear|not clear|unfair)' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SwayamBhageria/claims-overturn-bench/main/bench/grounds.py). 307 of 626 upheld cases (49%) matched no ground at all; the author calls the tag layer 'the least validated thing on the page' and the untagged share 'the tagger's recall problem' (https://github.com/SwayamBhageria/claims-overturn-bench; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SwayamBhageria/claims-overturn-bench/main/results/analysis.json). So the wording-interpretation share of upheld decisions is bounded between 2.6% and about 51%; among tagged cases it is 16/319 = 5.0%. A lexical floor with that ceiling cannot be 'the strongest datapoint' for anything. Separately, the corpus is a 0-star, 15-commit single-author repo built from full-text searches such as 'declined the claim', and it measures why an ombudsman overturns an insurer under the 'fair and reasonable' standard (28.6% of upheld left the decline intact and faulted handling), not why insurer staff review claims. It is a category error to use it as an H1 instrument for insurance claims review.

refuted.claim: H2: 'SUPPORTED at the granularity where disputes actually arise (fine classes, 86% singletons)'.
refuted.why: Two problems. (1) The repo's own recurrence.json carries a note the finder omitted: 'A 1,000-row sample of ~82,787 rows under-states recurrence in the full stream (sampling thins repeats), so treat fine-granularity figures as pessimistic and the ordering across granularities as the result' (file:///home/user/sophon/results/recurrence.json). What is true is that absolute volume is tiny (46 published reviews in 14 years); recurrence-of-ambiguity per se is not refuted by these data.

manual_review_conflated_with_repeatable_: FOS published decisions (the escalated tail after investigator stage, decided on 'fair and reasonable') were used as a measure of why insurers' claims staff review claims. They measure ombudsman overturn grounds, and 45% of those are handling remedies that arise from the ombudsman's remedial jurisdiction, not from claim-review drivers. No inference about the H share of insurer claims review can be drawn from them.

IPSA published appeal reviews (46 in 14 years) were used to bound H for expenses review as '2-15%'. They are selected disputes at the Compliance Officer tier; IPSA's internal validation reviews (the actual manual-review pool) are not public and no effort or reason data exists for them (repo follow-up document says so explicitly).

Prior authorisation 'human_review_rate: 100% of PA requests are human/clinician-touched on the denial side' restates a who-signs mandate, not a measure of why review occurs; and the finder then estimated A 5-40% for PA with no PA-specific data beyond the word 'often'.

IPSA recurrence classes (category, cost type, item text) are purchase classes, not ambiguity classes. A unique item text can be fully governed by one settled clause; the correct recurrence unit for H is the rule-clause question, at which the 46 disputes visibly cluster (cleaning exclusion x3, budget-year allocation x2, 'exceptional' x3, leaflets x4).
Permission-log 'settlements' (906 command classes) are access grants, not interpretive ambiguities; reuse of a grant class says nothing about whether an interpretation recurred.

Within the IPSA appeal tail, 20-25% of published disputes are rule-meaning questions that recur at clause level and could in principle be settled prospectively, but only IPSA (not the reviewer) can settle them and it did so in 4 of 17 recommended cases; within FOS upheld decisions the wording-interpretation share is a floor of 2.6% with a ceiling near 51% because of the tagger; for prior authorisation there is no number.

verification.overall: The finder's directional conclusions mostly survive, but three of its most quotable numbers do not. Refuted: the OpenFisca 'interpretation issues open for years' (the cited issues are metadata and parameter-freshness tickets; the one legal-reading issue closed in about ten months and the codebase releases several times a week), the FOS tool's '13% divided precedent' (a pre-registered abstention threshold, not a measure of ombudsman inconsistency), and 'policy wording 2.6%' as the strongest anti-thesis datapoint (a four-pattern regex floor with 49% of upheld cases untagged, from a 0-star repo, measuring ombudsman overturn grounds rather than insurer review drivers). Also omitted by the finder: the recurrence file's own warning that a 1.2% sample mechanically produces singletons, and the visible clause-level clustering of the 46 IPSA disputes, both of which cut in the thesis's favour on recurrence while confirming trivially low volume in that tail. Everything drawn from the local IPSA corpus study, the AHIP document and the two GitHub corpora was re-checked and is accurately transcribed. Net effect on the four hypotheses: H1 is untested rather than partially supported (no live review pool has a facts-vs-interpretation split); H2 is untested rather than supported (only low absolute volume in public tails is established); H3 is stronger against the product than reported (fast community encoding, DGFiP annual publication, state-run binding ledgers in tax/customs/social security, and the one open-source interpretation ledger parking itself for lack of demand); H4 keeps its direction for adverse consumer decisions but rests on unverified legal texts and a self-reported trade-body survey. The finder's recommendation to run the base-rate experiment where the decision owner holds rule-making power, on approvals, at coarse class granularity, remains sensible, with the added condition that the experiment must sample a live review pool, since no public appeal tail examined here can estimate the H share.
